articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This action modifies existing authorizations related to transactions involving Venezuela, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy in the region.

The specifics of the amendments and the new FAQ aim to provide clarity and guidance to individuals and entities engaging in or seeking to engage in certain transactions with Venezuela. These updates are crucial for ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions programs, which remain complex and subject to change based on evolving geopolitical circumstances.

Stakeholders are advised to review the updated GL and FAQ carefully to understand the scope of permitted activities and any new restrictions. OFAC's continuous adjustments to Venezuela sanctions underscore the dynamic nature of these measures and the need for diligent adherence to regulatory requirements.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran and Cuba, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 15, 2026. This action signifies a tightening of sanctions against entities and individuals connected to both nations.

Among the entities targeted in the Iran-related designations is Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), sanctioned due to its ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank, which has been under U.S. sanctions since 2020. The U.S. also imposed sanctions on the Iraq-based International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, citing its provision of financial services and U.S. dollar access for Iran.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez criticized the action as 'aggressive,' asserting that BICSA is a legitimate bank. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that 'Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups — including the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism — to target the United States.' The new sanctions package also includes 16 individuals and 11 entities, targeting financial institutions, currency exchange firms, and energy and trading companies.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a specific entity or individual previously subject to sanctions under the Venezuela program has been delisted.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in circumstances, a determination that the designated party no longer meets the criteria for designation, or as part of broader diplomatic or policy shifts.

While the specific details of the removed designation were not immediately provided, such actions are part of OFAC's ongoing management of its sanctions programs, which involve both additions and removals based on continuous review and assessment.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities on October 13, 2026. These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting illicit financial networks that support drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.

The designations aim to isolate these actors from the international financial system, preventing them from accessing resources that fuel their illicit operations. Such measures often involve freezing assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties.

These designations are part of a broader strategy to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist groups, highlighting the ongoing efforts to protect U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces International Criminal Court Designation and General Licenses; Burma-related Designation Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses (GLs) on October 9, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC also announced a Burma-related designation removal.

The ICC designation and accompanying GLs indicate a specific action taken in relation to individuals or entities associated with the International Criminal Court, with the GLs likely providing carve-outs or authorizations for certain activities. This reflects the U.S. government's nuanced approach to international legal bodies.

The removal of a Burma-related designation signifies a recalibration of sanctions against specific parties in Burma, potentially in response to changing political dynamics or compliance efforts within the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026. This GL authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the extensive Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to provide specific exemptions for activities deemed necessary or in the U.S. national interest, without undermining the broader sanctions objectives. This new GL will be important for entities navigating the complex landscape of Russia sanctions.
The issuance of new GLs reflects OFAC's ongoing efforts to manage the impact of sanctions while allowing for legitimate humanitarian, commercial, or other authorized activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and the issuance of an Iran-related General License (GL), alongside an amended Russia-related GL, on October 8, 2026. These actions highlight the U.S. government's dual focus on pressuring Iran while also adjusting its approach to sanctions against Russia.

The Iran-related designations target specific individuals or entities deemed to be supporting the Iranian regime, further restricting their access to the international financial system. The accompanying Iran-related GL may authorize certain humanitarian or other specific transactions.

The amendment to the Russia-related GL indicates a modification to existing authorizations for transactions involving Russia. This could either expand or narrow the scope of permitted activities, requiring careful review by affected parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ, Announces Designations Removals
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an alert warning foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that they could be targeted without advance notification if they continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions. This alert, issued on October 5, 2026, is part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched by OFAC on August 24, 2026, to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime.

Concurrently, OFAC amended Iran-related FAQ 156, removing language that previously indicated the Treasury Department would generally contact FFIs to inquire about their conduct before making a finding of sanctionable activity. The updated FAQ now refers to the alert, emphasizing the potential for immediate targeting. FFIs providing financial services to Iranian banks or their subsidiaries risk sanctions for supporting sanctioned sectors of Iran's economy.

In addition to these warnings, OFAC also announced several designations removals and updates. These removals indicate a recalibration of sanctions against specific entities, while the updates ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of the sanctions lists.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting or engaging in acts of terrorism, further strengthening the U.S. government's efforts to combat global terrorism.

These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist organizations by freezing assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from conducting transactions with the designated parties. This helps to cut off funding and resources vital for their operations.

The continuous imposition of counter terrorism sanctions reflects the ongoing threat posed by terrorist groups and the U.S. commitment to using financial tools to counter these threats and protect national security.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., imposing a civil penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty addresses 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred when Bank of America channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error, allowed designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, failed to promptly update watchlists, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons.

As a result of these compliance failures, Bank of America processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs. OFAC determined that the violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement amount reflects no reduction for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a record $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This penalty is the largest in OCC history and stems from the bank's deficient and ineffective BSA/AML compliance program.

The OCC found that Bank of America's transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to a large number of late Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars. Many of these late SARs showed indicia of money laundering, and the bank had known for years about its failure to escalate potentially suspicious activities for review.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, the OCC stated that Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance and continued to exhibit significant breakdowns in internal controls. The bank's BSA Officer and staff also lacked sufficient skills and expertise, and key personnel did not receive appropriate training, resulting in inaccurate and late SARs.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express on October 8, 2026. This action was taken in conjunction with a parallel consent order issued by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, addressing significant deficiencies in American Express's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs.

The OCC found that American Express's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training. Specifically, the bank's BSA/AML risk assessment focused too narrowly on its demand-deposit business, failing to adequately address risks associated with its much larger credit and charge-card business.

The enforcement actions highlight a broader focus on accountability and remediation, with the Federal Reserve's order requiring board oversight and senior management accountability, and the OCC's order coupling the penalty with extensive forward-looking remediation and an independent historical SAR review.

articles.headline: BIS Revises Entity List by Removing Two Addresses for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd.
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a revision to the Entity List, removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This final rule, effective August 21, 2026, follows the removal of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd. and six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

The Entity List identifies foreign entities subject to specific license requirements for the export, reexport, or transfer of U.S.-origin items due to national security or foreign policy concerns. Decisions regarding additions, removals, or modifications to the Entity List are made by the End-User Review Committee (ERC), composed of representatives from the Departments of Commerce, State, Defense, Energy, and Treasury.

While this specific action involves a removal, the Entity List remains a powerful tool in U.S. export enforcement, with almost all export enforcement actions in 2026 thus far stemming from Entity List violations. The lack of additions to the Entity List since October 2025 marks a departure from previous years, where additions were made every 35 days on average.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
